newsitem.title: ITALY: U.S. and British buyers pile into Milan bourse.
newsitem.headline: U.S. and British buyers pile into Milan bourse.

text.p: Heavy buying by U.S. and British funds is helping drive the Milan bourse to all-time highs as investors lay bets in the hope of reaping handsome profits if Italy succeeds in a bid to join a European currency union.
"International investors are doing most of the work," said James Cornish, European Market strategist at Natwest Markets in London.

The all-share Mibtel index, introduced in July 1993 with the launch of electronic screen-based trading, hit a new record high 14,817 on Thursday. The blue chip Mib30 index also jumped to an unprecedented 22,615.

The so-called Comit index, closely watched by fund managers and traders, looked poised to soar above a previous all-time high of 908.20 reached on May 20, 1986. The index, compiled daily after the close of trade by Banca Commerciale Italiana, closed at 896.68 on Wednesday.

"European economic and monetary union is the main factor. What makes Spain and Italy attractive is that there is room for interest rates to come down quite a bit further than other countries," Cornish added.

Driving the stock boom is a conviction among foreign investors that Italy's chances of joining EMU have never been greater as inflation tumbles and a tax squeeze cuts into a once ballooning public deficit.
Membership of a currency union would wipe out a single stroke one of the main risks of holding Italian stocks -- the fear of a sudden devaluation.
"The risk premium which traditionally applied to Italy is now much lower," said Michael Pacitti, an Italian equities specialist at James Capel in London.
Rising expectations that Italy will join EMU have held out the tanatalising promise of permanently lower interest rates.
"What makes countries like Spain and Italy attractive is the fact that there is room for interest rates to come down quite a bit further," said Cornish.

The market, which until recently was widely perceived as undervalued, still has some way to climb before runs out of steam. "There has been a re-rating of the Italian market. In the past it was undervalued compared to the rest of Europe," said Alberto Rolla, an analyst at Milan's Pasfin brokers.
"We see 970 on the Comit index as an objective," he added.

Investors also have more shares to pick from than ever before in a market that has traditionally been looked on with suspicion as a haven for insider trading with little to offer beyond a clutch of closely held family-run companies.
After a string of privatisations and initial public offerings (IPO) the range of stocks available to investors is now significantly greater than in the past.

State energy group ENI, floated in December 1995, is now the most liquid stock on the market while mobile phone operator Telecom Italia Mobile, listed two years ago, is another favourite with domestic and foreign investors.
"You have now got a better choice of stocks which are more representative of the economy," said Pacitti.
Smaller companies, which form the backbone of Italy's economy are also being lured by investment bankers to seek a stock exchange listing.
IPOs in July include hosiery company CSP International, rubber and metal components firm Manuli Rubber Industries and machinery company Idra Presse.
Aeroporti di Roma, the state company which runs Rome airports, is also floating up to 45 percent of its capital on the bourse, the first such offering in Italy of a company of this kind.
